summary: Summarizes request-routing techniques that content networks used on or before December 2000 to direct client requests to a suitable server. They fall into DNS, transport-layer, and application-layer methods. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A content network keeps copies of the same site in many places. Something has to decide which copy each visitor reaches, and this memo lists the mechanisms that were used for that.

questions: how cdn directs users to servers
how does dns based request routing work
what is url rewriting in a cdn
what are the drawbacks of dns request routing
subtitle: A survey of the ways a content network steered each client request to a suitable server.

tldr.problem: When the same content lives on many servers, something has to decide which one answers each client request.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sorts the known techniques into DNS request-routing, transport-layer request-routing and application-layer request-routing, and sets out the strengths and drawbacks of each, including anycast, 302 redirection, URL rewriting and the metrics used to pick a surrogate.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational survey of techniques commonly used on or before December 2000, not a specification, and it has been updated by RFC 8996.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Techniques in use on or before December 2000

today: RFC 3568 is an Informational RFC from July 2003. It is a survey of techniques commonly used on or before December 2000 and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, and it has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: What Request-Routing Is
sections.content:
Request-routing directs client requests to surrogates based on various policies and a possible set of metrics. The task of directing a client's request to a surrogate is also called content routing or content redirection, and the techniques are commonly used in Content Networks, also known as Content Delivery Networks. Content Networks include network infrastructure in layers 4 through 7 and deal with the routing and forwarding of requests and responses for content, relying on layer 7 protocols such as HTTP for transport.

A request-routing system uses a set of metrics in an attempt to direct users to the surrogate that can best serve the request. The choice of surrogate could be based on network proximity, bandwidth availability, surrogate load and availability of content. The memo covers techniques that were commonly used in the industry on or before December 2000, and classifies them at a high level as DNS request-routing, transport-layer request-routing and application-layer request-routing.
sections.plainLanguage: The same content is stored on many servers. Something has to pick the server that should answer each request, and the memo sorts the techniques that were used into three classes.

sections.title: DNS-Based Request-Routing
sections.content:
DNS-based techniques are common because of the ubiquity of the DNS. A specialized DNS server is inserted into the resolution process, and it can return a different set of A, NS or CNAME records based on user defined policies, metrics, or a combination of both.

With a single reply, the server returns the address of the best surrogate, which may be a virtual IP address standing for a set of surrogates. With multiple replies, it returns several A records, and common client-site DNS servers cycle through them in a round-robin fashion, so the order of the records can steer several clients using one client-site server.

Multi-level resolution brings several request-routing DNS servers into one resolution, so that a complex decision can be split between several specialized servers. The common mechanisms are NS and CNAME records. With NS redirection the number of request-routing servers is limited by the number of parts in the DNS name, the last DNS server can set the TTL of the whole resolution, and the extra lookups add delay; some implementations of bind also cause timeouts when an NS redirect points at a name server with no valid A record. With CNAME redirection the resolution moves to an entirely new domain, which adds the overhead of resolving that name, but the number of request-routing servers no longer depends on the format of the domain name.

Object encoding puts the object type, object hash or similar information into the DNS name, for example images.a.b.example.com or streaming.a.b.example.com. Object information is then available at resolution time, but the client-site DNS server has to perform multiple resolutions to retrieve a single Web page, which might increase rather than decrease the overall latency.
sections.plainLanguage: The address lookup system is used to make the choice. A specialized name server is inserted into the lookup and hands back the address of a good server instead of the usual one.

sections.title: Anycast and the Limits of DNS
sections.content:
With anycast, a request-routing DNS server advertises one anycast address that several physical DNS servers share, and the server closest to the client-site DNS server in terms of OSPF and BGP routing receives the query and can use that fact in its decision. The RFC lists the drawbacks: the DNS server may not be the closest server in terms of routing to the client, routing protocols are typically not load sensitive so the closest server may not have the least network latency, and server load is not considered during the request-routing process at all.

The RFC then lists the general limits of DNS-based routing. DNS only allows resolution at the domain level, while an ideal system should service requests per object. Servers may be required to return short TTL values so they can react quickly to outages, which in turn may increase the volume of DNS requests, and many DNS implementations do not honor the TTL field anyway. Request-routing is based only on knowledge of the client-side DNS server, because client addresses are not relayed within DNS requests, which limits the ability to judge a client's proximity to the surrogate. Users who share a single client-site DNS server are redirected to the same set of addresses for the length of the TTL, which might overload a surrogate during a flash crowd. The memo also warns that DNS-based techniques can overburden third party DNS servers, and points readers to RFC 2782 for guidance and warnings on using DNS for load balancing.
sections.plainLanguage: The address lookup system can only choose a whole domain, not a single file, and it cannot see the visitor's own address. It also often ignores how long it says an answer should be cached.

sections.title: Transport-Layer Request-Routing
sections.content:
At the transport layer a finer level of granularity is reached by close inspection of the client's requests. The request-routing system inspects the information available in the first packet of the client's request to make its surrogate selection decision. That inspection gives data about the client's IP address, port information and layer 4 protocol, which can be combined with user-defined policies and other metrics to select a surrogate better suited to serving the request. The techniques used to hand the session off to that surrogate are beyond the scope of the document.

In general, the forward-flow traffic from the client to the newly selected surrogate flows through the surrogate that DNS originally chose, while the reverse-flow traffic from the surrogate to the client, which normally transfers much more data, typically takes the direct path. The overhead of this approach is better suited to long-lived sessions such as FTP and RTSP, and it can also be used to direct clients away from overloaded surrogates. Transport-layer request-routing can be combined with DNS-based techniques: the DNS method resolves the request on a domain basis with exposure to the client-side DNS server address, and the transport-layer system then refines that first step.
sections.plainLanguage: The system looks at the first packet the visitor sends. That shows the visitor's address and the port, which is more detail than the address lookup system could offer.

sections.title: Application-Layer Request-Routing
sections.content:
Application-layer systems examine the client's packets beyond the transport-layer header, which gives fine-grained control down to the level of individual objects. The exposure to the client's IP address combined with the fine-grained knowledge of the requested objects lets these systems control the selection of the best surrogate much more closely.

Under header inspection, protocols such as HTTP, RTSP and SSL give hints in the initial portion of the session about how the request must be directed, from the URL of the content or from other parts of the request header such as cookies. In URL-based routing, the client's request is first resolved to a virtual surrogate, and the surrogate returns an application-specific code such as the 302, in the case of HTTP or RTSP, to redirect the client to the actual delivery node; the technique is relatively simple but the redirect adds latency. With an in-path element, the element sits in the forwarding path of the request, transparently intercepts the connection, examines the request and splices the client connection to the chosen delivery node, at the cost of URL parsing in the traffic path; it allows traffic to be partitioned among delivery nodes by content object, so that requests for non-cacheable object types can be directed away from a cache. Header-based routing uses fields such as Cookie, Language and User-Agent: cookies identify a customer or a session, the language header can direct traffic to a language-specific node, and the user-agent header helps identify the type of client device, such as a voice browser, a PDA or a cell phone.

Under content modification, the content provider takes direct control of the routing decision without switching devices or directory services in the path. Most web pages consist of an HTML document with references to embedded objects such as GIF or JPEG images, and the provider can modify those references so the client fetches them from the best surrogate; this is also known as URL rewriting. A-priori rewriting happens before the content is placed on the origin server and cannot take client specifics into account. On-demand rewriting happens when the request reaches the origin server, at which point the client is known, so an automated process can choose the surrogate that suits that client best. The limitations are that the first request from a client to a site must be served from the origin server, and rewritten pages should be marked as non-cacheable or cacheable only for a short time, because rewritten URLs on cached pages can become outdated and point to surrogates that are no longer available or no longer good choices. The memo notes that such modification must be consistent with RFC 3238.
sections.plainLanguage: These systems read the request itself, not just the address of the sender, so they can choose a server for each individual object. They can redirect the client with a 302 response, or splice the connection to the chosen server, or rewrite the object references inside the page before the client fetches them.

sections.title: Combining Mechanisms and Security
sections.content:
The memo gives one example of combining mechanisms. A basic problem of DNS request-routing is that its resolution granularity works per domain only, so a per-object redirection cannot easily be achieved. Content modification can overcome this: references to different objects on the same origin server can be rewritten to point into different domain name spaces, and DNS request-routing can then direct requests for those objects to different surrogates. Appendix A collects the metrics that can be used. Proximity here means round-trip time, measured in a DNS request-routing system to the client's local DNS server. Active probing, for example a periodic ICMP ECHO Request sent from each surrogate to a potential requester, has limits: measurements can only be taken periodically, firewalls and NATs disallow probes, and probes often set off intrusion detection systems. The metrics listed are latency, router hop counts and BGP information such as the AS PATH and MED attributes, though the RFC notes that AS PATH information can be meaningless as a good selection metric. Feedback for choosing a least-loaded node can come from probing with an HTTP request, which makes real-time information hard to obtain, or from agents that reside on the surrogates.

On security, the memo says that security must be addressed by any entity that implements a technique that redirects client requests, and points to RFC 3238 for the main requirements for entities that modify content. It recommends that implementers be aware of routing protocol security, because active probing techniques will set off intrusion detection systems and firewalls. It also notes the impact of TLS on request routing: when TLS is used, the full URL is not visible to the content network unless it terminates the TLS session.
sections.plainLanguage: Two mechanisms work better together than one: content modification can point each object at a different domain, and the DNS then sends each object to a different server. The appendix lists the measurements used to pick a server, including round-trip time, hop counts and BGP information.
